lesson.title: Punishing a Port: The Intolerable Acts
lesson.summary: Furious at the destruction of tea in Boston harbor, Parliament passed a series of punitive laws in 1774 meant to isolate Massachusetts, but they instead pushed the colonies toward unity.
lesson.body:
When news of the Boston Tea Party reached London in early 1774, Parliament responded with a set of laws designed to punish Massachusetts and reassert royal authority over a colony that seemed to be slipping out of control. Colonists soon began calling these measures the Intolerable Acts, though in Britain they were known officially as the Coercive Acts. The goal was to isolate Boston, make an example of it, and discourage other colonies from following its lead in defying Parliament.

The first and most immediate was the Boston Port Act, which closed the port of Boston to almost all shipping until the East India Company was repaid for the destroyed tea. Since Boston depended heavily on maritime trade for food, fuel, and income, this act threatened the city with economic strangulation almost overnight. The Massachusetts Government Act followed, effectively revoking the colony's long standing charter. It made the previously elected governor's council an appointed body instead, sharply restricted town meetings to one per year without official approval, and gave the royal governor far greater control over local government, undercutting a tradition of colonial self rule that Massachusetts had practiced for generations.

A third measure, the Administration of Justice Act, allowed royal officials accused of crimes committed while enforcing the law to be tried in Britain or in another colony rather than in Massachusetts itself. Colonists denounced this as the Murder Act, arguing it let soldiers and officials escape accountability for violence against colonists, a fear rooted in memories of the Boston Massacre. A new Quartering Act gave royal governors broader authority to house British troops in unoccupied buildings, reviving old grievances about the presence of a standing army among civilians.

Many colonists also lumped in the Quebec Act of 1774, passed around the same time though not strictly punitive in origin. It expanded the boundaries of the province of Quebec into the Ohio Valley, land several colonies claimed for themselves, and granted legal toleration to the Catholic Church there. Protestant colonists, already anxious about British intentions, saw it as further evidence that Parliament could redraw colonial governance and religious life on a whim, without any colonial input.

To enforce these laws, Britain appointed General Thomas Gage, commander of British forces in North America, as the new military governor of Massachusetts, putting a soldier directly in charge of civil government. Rather than isolating Massachusetts as Parliament intended, the Intolerable Acts convinced colonists across the other colonies that what had happened to Boston could happen to any of them. Other colonies sent food, money, and public support to the suffering port, and that shared fear did more than any prior grievance to unite the colonies and led directly to the calling of a Continental Congress.
